```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.8, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "pdmS7")
pal <- c(blue = "#236b83", orange = "#a26421", green = "#5b8c3a", grey = "#9aa7b0",
         dark = "#444444")
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", abs(100 * x))
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
```

A model built for flood warning is judged by its floods: whether the peaks come out the right
size and at the right time. A calibration is usually judged by something else, a single score
over the whole record. The two can disagree badly. This article explains why, and walks
through the tools in pdmS7 that bring the floods back into view:

1. **Finding the events** in the record, and setting aside the ones not to trust.
2. **Checking a calibration** for the warning signs a good score hides.
3. **Calibrating for events**, so that the search itself cares about the peaks.
4. **Looking at the events yourself**, and adjusting the model by eye, with every change
   logged.
5. **Asking whether the structure is right**, and what the record can and cannot say about it.

It is written for hydrologists rather than programmers: the code is there to show what is
run, but the text stands on its own. The example is a made-up catchment, so the truth is known
and every claim can be checked against it.

# The example catchment

The catchment is 40 km2, with three years of hourly rain and flow. Its true model responds
quickly, with surface stores of 2 and 3 hours, and delays its outflow by 3 hours. The flow is
measured with a small random error, as a gauge would.

```{r data}
rain <- synthetic_rain("2019-10-01", years = 3, dt = 1, seed = 21)
forcing <- data.frame(time = rain$time, rain = rain$rain, pet = rain$pet)
truth <- pdm_presets("standard")
truth$area_km2 <- 40
truth$surface$k1 <- 2
truth$surface$k2 <- 3
truth$td <- 3
truth$recharge$kg <- 1500
model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
set.seed(3)
observed <- run_pdm(model, forcing, initial_state_from_flow(model, 0.6, 0.7))$output$q_m3s *
  exp(stats::rnorm(nrow(forcing), 0, 0.04))
```

The calibration is kept in a project, as a real one would be: the first year warms the model
up, the second is for calibration, and the third, which no calibration sees, is for
validation.

```{r project, results="hide"}
options(pdmS7.user = "A Hydrologist", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
project <- file.path(tempdir(), "example-brook")
unlink(project, recursive = TRUE)
start_calibration_project(project, "Example Brook", "00001", "Floods article", 40,
                          "An Owner", "A Steward")
register_data(project, forcing, observed,
              calibration = c("2020-10-01", "2021-09-30 23:00"),
              validation = c("2021-10-01", "2022-09-30 23:00"), wettest_years = 0)
start <- pdm_presets("standard")
start$area_km2 <- 40
structure <- select_structure(project, start, "Standard PDM to start from")
```

# Why a good score can hide bad floods

The usual calibration fits the model in three stages: first the water balance and slow
flows, then the fast response, then everything together. Each is scored by the
Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), which compares the squared errors with the variance of the
flow. A perfect model scores 1.

```{r plain, results="hide"}
plain <- log_staged_calibration(project, structure$id, "The standard three stages.",
                                starts = 2, seed = 1, control = list(maxit = 30))
plain_fit <- plain[[length(plain)]]
propose_candidate(project, plain_fit$id, "Standard stages.")
validate_candidate(project, "Validation year.")
plain_checks <- calibration_checks(project, top = 10)
```

```{r plain-numbers, include=FALSE}
plain_nse <- read_entry(project, plain_fit$id)$scores$nse
plain_val <- plain_checks$summary[plain_checks$summary$period == "validation", ]
plain_k <- plain_checks$parameters$value[plain_checks$parameters$path == "surface.k1"]
```

The result scores `r f2(plain_nse)`. By most standards that is a good calibration. Yet on
the ten largest floods of the validation year, the median peak is
`r pct(plain_val$median_peak_error)` too low and comes `r abs(plain_val$median_timing_error_h)`
hours early, and only `r round(10 * plain_val$share_peak_within_20pct)` of the ten peaks lies
within 20% of what was measured.

How can both be true? NSE counts every hour equally. In a year there are 8,760 hours, and a
flood peak occupies a handful of them. The long recessions and quiet spells between storms
make up almost all of the score. A model can get those right, put every peak a little out in
time and well short, and still score 0.9.

There is a second, quieter problem. The true model delays its outflow by 3 hours, but the
standard stages hold the time delay at zero. Unable to move the peaks later, the search did
the next best thing: it slowed both surface stores, to `r f2(plain_k)` hours each, so the
flood arrives later but spread out and lower. The parameters have been bent to make up for
something the search could not change. They no longer describe the catchment, and they will
mislead anyone who reads them as if they did.

# Finding the events

To judge a model on its floods, first find them. Doing it by hand is slow and inconsistent
across hydrologists, and impossible across hundreds of catchments.
[`find_events()`](../reference/find_events.html) does it objectively, with the method of
Giani and others (2022). It needs only rain and flow.

It works in three steps:

- **The catchment's response time.** It estimates how long, typically, flow takes to answer
  rain. This sets the scale on which a burst of rain counts as one storm.
- **Rain and flow windows.** For each storm it marks the rain window, from the first rain to
  the last, and the flow window, from where the flow starts to rise to where it has fallen
  back.
- **A baseflow line.** It draws a line joining the start and end points of every event. Flow
  above the line is the event's quick flow; flow below it is baseflow, the river's slow
  background supply.

```{r events, fig.cap="Part of the calibration year. Shaded: the flow windows of the events found. Dashed: the baseflow line beneath them."}
events <- find_events(forcing$rain, observed, forcing$time, dt = 1, area_km2 = 40)
nrow(events)
attr(events, "response")$response_h
shown <- which(forcing$time >= as.POSIXct("2020-12-01", tz = "UTC") &
                 forcing$time < as.POSIXct("2021-01-15", tz = "UTC"))
par(mar = c(2.5, 4.2, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(forcing$time[shown], observed[shown], type = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)", las = 1)
inside <- events[events$flow_start %in% shown, ]
for (i in seq_len(nrow(inside))) {
  rect(forcing$time[inside$flow_start[i]], 0, forcing$time[inside$flow_end[i]], 1e3,
       col = adjustcolor(pal[["blue"]], 0.12), border = NA)
}
lines(forcing$time[shown], observed[shown], col = pal[["dark"]])
lines(forcing$time[shown], attr(events, "baseflow")[shown], col = pal[["orange"]], lty = 2,
      lwd = 1.5)
```

**How the method finds them.** The response time is the average lag between the centre of
mass of rain and the centre of mass of the flow it produces. Rain and flow are each
accumulated, and each cumulative series has its moving average subtracted, leaving its
fluctuations. Over a window about twice the response time the two are most strongly
anti-correlated, and that window gives the estimate (Giani and others, 2021). At that window
an event is under way wherever both rain and flow fluctuate: each such stretch is an event's
core, its edges are moved out to where the rain starts and stops and the flow starts to rise
and finishes receding, and events that do not fit are dropped or merged. The one setting is
`rain_min`, the smallest rain intensity that counts: by default 0.2 mm/h at an hourly step,
the authors' guidance for British catchments.

The response time is not a time to peak. It is the timescale of the fast response: on
constructed records it recovers the centre of mass of a symmetric response exactly, and falls
short of one with a long recession tail. Use it to compare like with like, a catchment's
observed and simulated flow, or catchments with each other.

**One event per flood.** Calibration counts each flood once (`independent = TRUE`), by the rule
of UK peaks-over-threshold series: two peaks are separate floods only if they are at least
three response times apart and the flow between them falls below two-thirds of the smaller.
Otherwise the fragments of one long flood would each count as an event.

The method finds every burst of rain that moves the flow, small ones included: dozens of
events a year. [Many catchments](large-sample.html#events-across-a-sample) finds and scores
the events of a whole batch at once.

# Setting aside the events not to trust

Not every event deserves equal weight. A hydrologist calibrating by eye ignores some without
thinking: a "flood" that is only a ripple on a high baseflow, a storm the rain gauges plainly
missed, a hydrograph with half its data gone. The optimiser has no such instinct.
[`screen_events()`](../reference/screen_events.html) supplies it, with four flags:

| Flag | What it means | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Small rise | The peak rises less than a set share (20% by default) above the baseflow under it | On a high baseflow, a few percent of noise moves such a peak by hours; its size and timing say little |
| Quick flow above rain | More water ran off quickly than fell as rain | The rain record must be wrong for this event |
| Gaps | More than a tenth of the flow window is missing | The peak may be in the gap |
| Above the gauging | The peak is higher than any flow ever gauged | The rating is extrapolated, so the size is uncertain; the timing is still sound |

The first three leave an event out of the scores; the last only flags it, because the largest
floods are usually the ones that matter most, and a rating that gets their size wrong still
gets their order and timing right.

Every test works on the flow above the baseflow line, never on total flow. That matters in
groundwater-fed catchments, where a high, steady baseflow would otherwise count as runoff and
make every event look wetter than its rain, or hide genuine rises.

```{r screen}
screened <- screen_events(events, observed)
table(ifelse(screened$flags == "", "kept, no flags", screened$flags))
```

Every event set aside here is a small rise: real enough, but too small on the baseflow beneath
it to judge a peak by.

# Checking a calibration

Before accepting any calibration, two questions are worth more than its score.
[`calibration_checks()`](../reference/calibration_checks.html) answers both.

**Did any parameter end at the edge of its search range?** A parameter that runs into the
limit it was allowed is usually being pushed there to make up for something the structure
cannot do. It has stopped describing the catchment. This is the single clearest warning sign
in automatic calibration. A lower limit of zero, such as no time delay, is a natural floor
rather than a limit someone chose, and is not flagged.

**How does the model do on the largest events in each window?** For the ten largest events in
the calibration year, the validation year and any years outside both, it gives the median
peak error, the median timing error, how many peaks fall within 20% of the measured, and the
median NSE within each event.

```{r checks}
plain_checks$parameters[, c("path", "value", "lower", "upper", "at_bound")]
plain_checks$summary
```

Here no parameter is at a bound, so the first check passes. The second fails plainly: peaks
`r pct(plain_val$median_peak_error)` low and early in both years. A good score, a clean set of
parameters, and a model that is wrong where it matters. Only the event check catches it.

In a real calibration of a 37 km2 catchment, the same checks caught a worse case: an NSE of
0.90 over nine years, three of seven parameters pressed against their limits, and the largest
flood 47% too low and 16 hours late. The search had shut off the groundwater path and routed
every flood through the slow stores.

# Calibrating for events

The checks find the problem. The remedy is to let the search care about the floods.
`pdm_stages(events = TRUE)` adds a fourth stage after the usual three.

**What it changes.** Only the parts of the model that shape a flood: the two surface stores,
the store shape `b` that sets how fast runoff responds to wetting, and the time delay `td`,
searched from 0 to 6 hours. The soil and groundwater stores stay as the first three stages
left them, so the water balance, already settled, is not disturbed.

**What it aims at.** The largest half of the calibration events, after screening, scored on
three things at once:

- **How well each event's hydrograph matches**: an NSE pooled over the events, where each
  event is compared with its own average flow, so the long quiet spells between floods no
  longer count;
- **How far each peak is off**, as a share of the measured peak;
- **How far each peak is out in time**, measured in units of the catchment's response time,
  so that an hour matters more in a fast catchment than a slow one.

The first counts fully and the other two half each, by default.

## Which events

By default the events stage fits the largest half of the calibration events, by observed peak
(`event_share = 0.5`). A share is simple but arbitrary: in a wet record half the events
includes floods that matter, in a dry one it reaches down into ripples. A flow says what
matters directly. `event_share` can name one:

| `event_share` | Fits every event whose observed peak reaches |
|---|---|
| `0.5` (default) | the largest half, whatever their size |
| `"0.5QMED"` | half the median annual flood, near the threshold of a UK peaks-over-threshold series |
| `"QMED"` | the median annual flood: a handful of events in a decade |
| `"Q1"` | the flow exceeded 1 per cent of the time |
| `"Flood Warning"` | a threshold registered with the project, or a multiple of one such as `"0.8Flood Warning"` |
| `c(peak = 12)` | 12 m3/s |

The markers come from the record itself ([`flow_markers()`](../reference/flow_markers.html)):
QMED is the median of the water-year maxima, October to September, as in the Flood Estimation
Handbook, and `Q1` the flow exceeded 1 per cent of the time. A project with no registered
thresholds registers QMED, Q1 and Q5 itself, worked out from the calibration window alone, so
the validation and test data never shape them. Here are this catchment's:

```{r markers}
markers <- suppressWarnings(flow_markers(observed, dt = 1, time = forcing$time,
                                         markers = c("QMED", "0.5QMED", "Q1", "Q5")))
markers
peaks <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(events)), function(i) {
  max(observed[events$flow_start[i]:events$flow_end[i]], na.rm = TRUE)
}, numeric(1))
data.frame(marker = markers$name, events_reaching = vapply(markers$value,
                                                           function(q) sum(peaks >= q), 0))
```

A floor that only a few events reach gives the search too little to learn from, and the fit
can rest on luck; QMED alone suits a long record. `0.5QMED` is a sensible first choice. The
objective's description in the log says which events it fitted and why.


**How it searches.** The timing part changes in whole steps: a peak is either one hour late or
two, never 1.3. A search that feels for the slope of the ground finds no slope on a staircase,
so this stage uses dynamically dimensioned search (DDS), which tries points instead.

```{r events-stage, results="hide"}
stages <- pdm_stages(start, events = TRUE, event_budget = 150)
with_events <- log_staged_calibration(project, structure$id, "Stages with an events stage.",
                                      stages = stages, starts = 2, seed = 1,
                                      control = list(maxit = 30))
event_fit <- with_events[[length(with_events)]]
propose_candidate(project, event_fit$id, "Events stage.")
validate_candidate(project, "Validation year.")
event_checks <- calibration_checks(project, top = 10)
```

```{r events-numbers}
fitted <- read_entry(project, event_fit$id)$configuration
val <- function(chk) chk$summary[chk$summary$period == "validation", ]
data.frame(
  calibration = c("standard stages", "with the events stage"),
  nse = c(plain_nse, read_entry(project, event_fit$id)$scores$nse),
  median_peak_error = c(val(plain_checks)$median_peak_error,
                        val(event_checks)$median_peak_error),
  median_timing_error_h = c(val(plain_checks)$median_timing_error_h,
                            val(event_checks)$median_timing_error_h),
  peaks_within_20pct = c(val(plain_checks)$share_peak_within_20pct,
                         val(event_checks)$share_peak_within_20pct),
  time_delay_h = c(0, fitted$td)
)
```

The events stage found a time delay of `r f2(fitted$td)` hours, against a true 3. With the
delay free to do its job, the surface stores no longer need to stretch, and the peaks in the
validation year, which the calibration never saw, come out right in size and timing. The
overall NSE rose too. The two aims were never really in conflict here; the standard stages
simply could not reach the one parameter that mattered.

Real catchments will rarely be this tidy. If the structure cannot produce the floods at all,
no objective will make it, and the events stage will then show the problem more starkly
rather than hide it. That is still worth knowing.

Two more options belong here. `pdm_stages(thresholds = ...)` adds a score for crossing the
flood warning flows at the right times to the last stage: it rewards issuing warnings when
the river does cross them, and not otherwise. And every stage, including this one, is logged
in the project, with what it searched and what it found.

# Looking at the events yourself

Scores summarise; they do not show. A hydrologist learns most by looking at the floods,
changing something, and looking again. The events workbench makes that fast enough to be
natural, and keeps a record of it.

[`event_workbench()`](../reference/event_workbench.html) gathers a run's largest events, ten
unless you choose another number. `workbench_try()` reruns them with some parameters changed,
and `plot_workbench()` draws them before (blue) and after (vermillion), each with its peak and
timing errors in its title. Here the standard calibration is given the time delay it lacked:

```{r workbench, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="The six largest calibration events of the standard calibration (blue), and the same with a 3-hour delay and faster stores (vermillion). Black dots: observed. Bars at the top: rain."}
wb <- event_workbench(project, entry = plain_fit$id, n = 6)
wb
fixed <- workbench_try(wb, c(td = 3, surface.k1 = 2, surface.k2 = 3))
plot_workbench(wb, fixed)
```

The timing is now right, but the peaks overshoot a little. The other parameters were fitted
around the old, slow stores, and changing the stores alone leaves them out of step. That is
why the events stage refits the stores, `b` and the delay together, and why the workbench is
for looking and adjusting by eye, not for replacing the search.

**Why it is quick.** Rerunning three years of hourly data takes a fraction of a second, but a
16-year record at 15 minutes takes longer, and dragging a slider calls for an answer at
once. The workbench runs the record once and saves the state of the model just before each
event: how full each store was. A change to the surface stores or the time delay then reruns
only the events, each from its saved state. Each rerun starts a little before its event, long
enough for the fast stores to settle to the new settings, and the result is identical to
rerunning the whole record. A change that reaches the soil store, such as `b`, changes the
state before every event, so the workbench reruns the whole record instead.

**In the app.** The Events tab of [`calibration_app()`](../reference/calibration_app.html)
puts this on sliders: choose how many events to show and from which year, move the surface
stores, the time delay or `b`, and the events redraw. When you have a setting you believe,
**Save as trial** writes it to the project log with your verdict and your reasons, exactly as
a trial on the main Trial tab is written. A reviewer later sees what you changed, what it did,
and why you kept it. [Tailoring calibration to the largest events in the
app](app-events.html) walks through it step by step, with screenshots.

# Is the structure right?

Calibration tunes the numbers inside a structure. Sometimes the structure itself is the
problem: the shape of the soil store, the way groundwater is recharged, or the way it
drains. pdmS7 offers several of each. Choosing among them raises a harder question than
tuning: can the record tell them apart at all?

## Recessions: how the river empties

Between storms, once the fast stores have drained, the river is fed by groundwater alone, and
the way the flow falls says something about the groundwater store. Plot how fast the flow
falls against how high it is, both on log scales, and the points lie along a line. In theory
its slope is 1 for a linear store, 1.67 for the standard cubic store and 2 for an exponential
one. [`recession_analysis()`](../reference/recession_analysis.html) measures it.

```{r recession, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="How fast the flow falls against how high it is, from dry spells only. Dotted lines: the slopes of the linear, cubic and exponential stores."}
recession <- recession_analysis(observed, forcing$rain, dt = 1, time = forcing$time,
                                boot = 100)
recession
plot_recession(recession)
```

The true store here is cubic, yet the measured slope is `r f2(recession$slope)`, nowhere near
1.67, and consistent with none of the stores. The reason is that recharge does not stop when
the rain does. The soil keeps draining into groundwater through every recession, topping it
up, so the flow falls more slowly than the store alone would let it. On made-up catchments
where recharge did stop between storms, the slope recovered every store correctly; where it
did not, every store looked roughly linear.

So the recession plot is a check, not a selector. Its real use is to set a calibrated model's
recessions beside the record's (`plot_recession()` draws both, and the workbench's **Check
recessions** button does it in the app). If the model's low flows fall at a different rate
from the river's, they are right for the wrong reason.

## What the record can tell apart

To learn which structural choices a record can actually make, the package was tested on
made-up catchments where the true structure is known: each was calibrated with every option,
and scored on a year it had not seen.

```{r identification}
stores <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "recession_stores.csv", package = "pdmS7"))
rules <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "recharge_rules.csv", package = "pdmS7"))
margin <- function(d, groups) {
  cases <- split(d, d[groups], drop = TRUE)
  vapply(cases, function(x) {
    s <- sort(x$val_log_nse, decreasing = TRUE)
    s[1] - s[2]
  }, numeric(1))
}
found <- function(d, groups) {
  cases <- split(d, d[groups], drop = TRUE)
  vapply(cases, function(x) x$candidate[which.max(x$val_log_nse)] == x$truth[1], logical(1))
}
data.frame(
  choice = c("groundwater store (4 options)", "recharge rule (3 options)"),
  catchments = c(length(found(stores, c("truth", "recharge", "seed"))),
                 length(found(rules, c("truth", "seed")))),
  true_option_found = c(sum(found(stores, c("truth", "recharge", "seed"))),
                        sum(found(rules, c("truth", "seed")))),
  typical_winning_margin = c(stats::median(margin(stores, c("truth", "recharge", "seed"))),
                             stats::median(margin(rules, c("truth", "seed"))))
)
```

Both choices were found every time, but the margins tell two different stories. The
recharge rule won by a wide margin: a wrong rule changes when groundwater fills, and that
shows in every recession and every low flow. The groundwater store won by a hair, a few
thousandths of a point. These records came from the very model being fitted, with little
noise. Real records carry rain errors and a structure that is never exactly right, and a
margin of a few thousandths will not survive them.

The lesson is practical. Test the recharge rule; the record has something to say about it.
Do not expect the record to choose the groundwater store, and keep the standard cubic store
unless another is clearly better.

## Choosing one part at a time

Comparing every combination of soil store, recharge rule and groundwater store would mean
sixty calibrations. [`recommend_structure()`](../reference/recommend_structure.html) chooses
one part at a time instead, in the order the record can best answer: recharge first, then the
soil store, then the groundwater store. Each step compares its options on the validation year
and follows one rule:

1. Set aside any option that ended with a parameter at the edge of its range.
2. Treat every option within a small margin of the best score (0.02 by default) as equally
   good.
3. If the option already in use is among them, keep it: the record cannot justify a change.
4. Otherwise take the one whose largest validation floods are closest in size, then the one
   with fewer parameters.

```{r recommend, eval=FALSE}
recommend_structure(project, reasoning = "First choice of structure for Example Brook.")
```

Rule 3 makes it cautious on purpose. Where the record is silent, which for the groundwater
store is usual, the standard structure stays, and the note written to the project log says
so. A recommendation that changed the structure on a margin of 0.003 would be worse than
none.

# Putting it together

For a new catchment, a sensible order is:

1. **Register the data** in a project, with calibration and validation years, and the
   highest gauged flow if you know it.
2. **Look at the events** with `find_events()` and `screen_events()`. How many are there, and
   how many survive screening? If few do, as on a chalk stream, judge the model on its low
   flows and volumes instead.
3. **Calibrate in stages, with the events stage** if floods matter: `pdm_stages(events =
   TRUE)`, adding warning thresholds if you have them.
4. **Run the checks**: `calibration_checks()`. No parameter at a bound, and peaks and timing
   acceptable in the validation year, before anything else.
5. **Look at the floods** in the workbench, adjust by eye where the checks or your knowledge
   say so, and save what you keep as trials, with reasons.
6. **Question the structure** if the checks keep failing: `recommend_structure()`, with the
   recession plot as a check on the low flows.
7. **Validate and test**, and propose the result for sign-off as usual.

The script for Beggearn Huish follows this order: capped surface stores, the events stage,
optional thresholds, and the acceptance checks printed and saved at the end.

# What this cannot do

- **It cannot fix the rain.** If the gauges miss the storm, no model and no calibration will
  find the flood. Screening sets aside the worst cases; it cannot repair them.
- **It cannot fix the rating.** A peak above the highest gauging may be wrong in size. The
  model may be right and the record wrong.
- **It cannot make a structure do what it cannot.** The events stage and the workbench tune
  the response; they do not give the model a pathway it lacks.
- **The tests are synthetic.** The findings on what a record can tell apart come from
  made-up catchments where the structure was exactly right. They show what is possible at
  best. Real catchments will tell us how much survives.

# Terms

| Term | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| Event | One storm and the flood it produced: a rain window and a flow window |
| Response time | How long the flow typically takes to answer rain |
| Baseflow | The slow background flow, from groundwater; the dashed line under the events |
| Quick flow | Flow above the baseflow line during an event |
| Recession | The fall of the flow after rain stops |
| Bound | The edge of the range a parameter is allowed to search |
| NSE | Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the average flow |
| Validation | Scoring on a period the calibration did not see |

# References
